title: Die drei Brüder
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 124. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 124 is a tidy little contest: a father who cannot bear to favor one of his three sons over the others sends them off to take up a trade, promising the house to whichever comes home with the finest feat of skill. A barber lathers and shaves a running hare without a nick, a smith reshoes a galloping horse mid-stride, and a fencer stays bone-dry in a downpour by parrying every raindrop with his sword — and the father, unable to choose, simply lets all three keep the house together. There is no villain here and no real danger, only craftsmanship shown off at speed.

sentences.t: Es war ein Mann, der hatte drei Söhne und weiter nichts im Vermögen als das Haus, worin er wohnte.
sentences.l: There was a man, he had three sons and nothing further in property than the house in which he lived.
sentences.i: There was once a man who had three sons and no property beyond the house he lived in.
sentences.n: German often carries on with a demonstrative — “der hatte,” literally “that one had” — where English uses a relative “who”; the literal keeps the two-clause shape. “Vermögen” is everything a person owns, not money alone.

sentences.t: Nun hätte jeder gerne nach seinem Tode das Haus gehabt, dem Vater war aber einer so lieb als der andere, da wußte er nicht wie ers anfangen sollte, daß er keinem zu nahe thät;
sentences.l: Now each would gladly have had the house after his death, but to the father the one was as dear as the other, so he did not know how he should set about it that he did no one a wrong;
sentences.i: Now each of them would gladly have had the house after the father’s death, but the father held one as dear as another, and he did not know how to manage it so as to wrong none of them;
sentences.n: “dem Vater war einer so lieb als der andere” is built on a dative — literally “to the father one was as dear as the other.” “ers” = er es; “thät” is thun (modern tun) in the past subjunctive, “would do”; “einem zu nahe thun” means to do someone an injury.

sentences.t: verkaufen wollte er das Haus auch nicht, weils von seinen Voreltern war, sonst hätte er das Geld unter sie getheilt.
sentences.l: sell the house he did not want to either, because it was from his forebears, otherwise he would have divided the money among them.
sentences.i: nor did he wish to sell the house, since it came down from his forebears; otherwise he would have divided the money among them.
sentences.n: The infinitive stands first — “verkaufen wollte er” — a common way of putting the action in the spotlight. “weils” = weil es; “getheilt” is the 1857 spelling of geteilt.

sentences.t: Da fiel ihm endlich ein Rath ein und er sprach zu seinen Söhnen „geht in die Welt und versucht euch und lerne jeder sein Handwerk, wenn ihr dann wiederkommt, wer das beste Meisterstück macht, der soll das Haus haben.“
sentences.l: Then at last a counsel occurred to him and he spoke to his sons “go into the world and try yourselves and let each learn his trade; when you then come back again, whoever makes the best masterpiece, he shall have the house.”
sentences.i: Then at last a plan came to him, and he said to his sons: “Go out into the world and try yourselves, and let each of you learn a trade; and when you come back again, whoever makes the best masterpiece shall have the house.”
sentences.n: “einfallen” — a thought “falls in” to a person (dative ihm): it occurs to him, with the particle ein at the end. “Rath” (modern Rat) here is an expedient, a way out, rather than advice. A “Meisterstück” was the piece of work by which a journeyman proved himself a master of his guild; the whole tale hangs on that word.

sentences.t: Das waren die Söhne zufrieden, und der älteste wollte ein Hufschmied, der zweite ein Barbier, der dritte aber ein Fechtmeister werden.
sentences.l: With that the sons were content, and the eldest wanted to become a farrier, the second a barber, but the third a fencing-master.
sentences.i: The sons were content with that, and the eldest wished to become a farrier, the second a barber, and the third a fencing-master.
sentences.n: “Das waren die Söhne zufrieden” puts the thing agreed to first, in the accusative — an older turn where modern German would say “damit waren die Söhne zufrieden.” All three are trades: a Hufschmied shoes horses, a Barbier was a barber-surgeon who shaved and also bled patients and drew teeth, a Fechtmeister taught swordsmanship for a living. “werden” at the end governs all three.

sentences.t: Darauf bestimmten sie eine Zeit, wo sie wieder nach Haus zusammen kommen wollten, und zogen fort.
sentences.l: Thereupon they fixed a time when they wanted to come home together again, and drew away.
sentences.i: Thereupon they fixed a time when they would come home together again, and set out.
sentences.n: “wo” here means “when” — usual in older German for a point in time. “fortziehen,” to draw forth, is the ordinary word for setting out on the road.

sentences.t: Es traf sich auch, daß jeder einen tüchtigen Meister fand, wo er was rechtschaffenes lernte.
sentences.l: It happened too that each found a capable master, with whom he learned something proper.
sentences.i: And it fell out that each of them found a good master, with whom he learned his trade properly.
sentences.n: “es traf sich” — it so fell out. “was” = etwas; “rechtschaffenes” of a craft means solid, respectable work.

sentences.t: Der Schmied mußte des Königs Pferde beschlagen und dachte „nun kann dirs nicht fehlen, du kriegst das Haus.“
sentences.l: The smith had to shoe the king’s horses and thought “now it cannot fail you, you get the house.”
sentences.i: The smith was set to shoeing the king’s horses, and thought: “Now you cannot go wrong — the house is yours.”
sentences.n: “des Königs Pferde” — the genitive stands before its noun, as in English “the king’s horses.” “dirs” = dir es; “es kann dir nicht fehlen” is “you cannot fail.” He addresses himself as “you,” which the tales do whenever someone thinks to himself.

sentences.t: Der Barbier rasierte lauter vornehme Herren und meinte auch das Haus wäre schon sein.
sentences.l: The barber shaved nothing but grand gentlemen and thought too the house were already his.
sentences.i: The barber shaved none but gentlemen of rank, and he too reckoned the house as good as his.
sentences.n: “lauter” = nothing but, only. “wäre” is the subjunctive of reported thought — the sentence keeps its distance from the claim, which English does with “reckoned.”

sentences.t: Der Fechtmeister kriegte manchen Hieb, biß aber die Zähne zusammen und ließ sichs nicht verdrießen, denn er dachte bei sich „fürchtest du dich vor einem Hieb, so kriegst du das Haus nimmermehr.“
sentences.l: The fencing-master got many a blow, but bit his teeth together and did not let it vex him, for he thought to himself “if you are afraid of a blow, then you will never get the house.”
sentences.i: The fencing-master took many a blow, but he set his teeth and did not let it discourage him, for he thought to himself: “If you flinch at a blow, you will never get the house.”
sentences.n: “fürchtest du dich …, so …” makes a condition by putting the verb first, with no “wenn” — English needs “if.” “sich etwas nicht verdrießen lassen” is to refuse to be put out by a thing. “Hieb” here is the noun, a blow or cut, not the past tense of hauen.

sentences.t: Als nun die gesetzte Zeit herum war, kamen sie bei ihrem Vater wieder zusammen;
sentences.l: When now the set time was round, they came together again at their father’s;
sentences.i: When the appointed time had come round, they gathered again at their father’s;
sentences.n: “herum sein,” of time, is to be up, to have run its course. “bei ihrem Vater” = at their father’s place.

sentences.t: sie wußten aber nicht wie sie die beste Gelegenheit finden sollten, ihre Kunst zu zeigen, saßen beisammen und rathschlagten.
sentences.l: but they did not know how they should find the best occasion to show their art, sat together and took counsel.
sentences.i: but they did not know how they might best find occasion to show their skill, so they sat together and took counsel.
sentences.n: “Kunst” is a craftsman’s skill here, not art in the modern sense. “rathschlagten” is the 1857 spelling of ratschlagten, from Rath (Rat): to deliberate together.

sentences.t: Wie sie so saßen, kam auf einmal ein Hase übers Feld daher gelaufen.
sentences.l: As they sat so, all at once a hare came running along across the field.
sentences.i: As they sat there, a hare suddenly came running across the field.
sentences.n: “daher gelaufen kommen” — German puts the manner into a participle and lets kommen carry the motion, which English does with “come running.”

sentences.t: „Ei,“ sagte der Barbier, „der kommt wie gerufen,“
sentences.l: “Well now,” said the barber, “he comes as if called,”
sentences.i: “Aha,” said the barber, “he comes just when he is wanted,”
sentences.n: “wie gerufen kommen” is still the everyday idiom for arriving at exactly the right moment. The sentence runs on into what follows without repeating its subject.

sentences.t: nahm Becken und Seife, schaumte so lange, bis der Hase in die Nähe kam,
sentences.l: [he] took basin and soap, lathered so long until the hare came near,
sentences.i: and he took basin and soap and worked up a lather until the hare came close,
sentences.n: The German does not repeat the subject — it is still the barber from the sentence before — so “[he]” is supplied here in square brackets to let the English stand. The Becken is the barber’s shaving basin, his trade sign as much as his tool.

sentences.t: dann seifte er ihn in vollem Laufe ein, und rasierte ihm auch in vollem Laufe ein Stutzbärtchen, und dabei schnitt er ihn nicht und that ihm an keinem Haare weh.
sentences.l: then he soaped him at full run, and shaved him, likewise at full run, a little trimmed beard, and in doing it he did not cut him and did him no hurt on a single hair.
sentences.i: then he soaped the hare at full gallop and, still at full gallop, shaved him a neat little beard, and never cut him nor hurt a hair of him.
sentences.n: “einseifen,” to soap up, with the particle ein at the end. In “rasierte ihm … ein Stutzbärtchen” the dative ihm marks the one it is done to, which English renders with a possessive or with “for him.” “that” = thun (modern tun); “weh thun” is to hurt.

sentences.t: „Das gefällt mir,“ sagte der Vater, „wenn sich die andern nicht gewaltig angreifen, so ist das Haus dein.“
sentences.l: “That pleases me,” said the father, “if the others do not exert themselves mightily, then the house is yours.”
sentences.i: “That I like,” said the father; “unless the others put out all their strength, the house is yours.”
sentences.n: “sich angreifen” in this older sense is to exert oneself, to strain every nerve — not to attack. “gefallen” runs from the thing to the person: the thing pleases me.

sentences.t: Es währte nicht lang, so kam ein Herr in einem Wagen daher gerennt in vollem Jagen.
sentences.l: It lasted not long, then came a gentleman in a carriage racing along at full chase.
sentences.i: It was not long before a gentleman came racing along in a carriage at full speed.
sentences.n: “es währte nicht lang, so …” is the older way of saying “it was not long before …”. “in vollem Jagen” = at full gallop; the tale repeats “in vollem Laufe / Jagen” for each brother’s feat, and the repetition is part of the joke.

sentences.t: „Nun sollt ihr sehen, Vater, was ich kann,“ sprach der Hufschmied,
sentences.l: “Now you shall see, father, what I can do,” spoke the farrier,
sentences.i: “Now, father, you shall see what I can do,” said the farrier,
sentences.n: “was ich kann” — können stands without an infinitive: what I am able to do. “sprach” is the tales’ narrative word for “said,” and you will meet it constantly.

sentences.t: sprang dem Wagen nach, riß dem Pferd, das in einem fort jagte, die vier Hufeisen ab und schlug ihm auch im Jagen vier neue wieder an.
sentences.l: [he] sprang after the carriage, tore the four horseshoes off the horse, which raced on without stopping, and struck four new ones on it again, likewise at the gallop.
sentences.i: and he sprang after the carriage, tore the four shoes off the horse as it galloped on without a pause, and hammered four new ones on again, still at the gallop.
sentences.n: The subject is again left out, and is supplied here in square brackets as “[he]”. Two separable verbs frame the sentence — abreißen (riß … ab) and anschlagen (schlug … an) — with the whole feat packed in between them. “in einem fort” = without stopping.

sentences.t: „Du bist ein ganzer Kerl,“ sprach der Vater, „du machst deine Sachen so gut, wie dein Bruder;
sentences.l: “You are a whole fellow,” spoke the father, “you do your things as well as your brother;
sentences.i: “You are a proper fellow,” said the father; “you do your work as well as your brother;
sentences.n: “ein ganzer Kerl” — a man of full worth; it is praise, not measurement.

sentences.t: ich weiß nicht wem ich das Haus geben soll.“
sentences.l: I do not know to whom I shall give the house.”
sentences.n: “wem” is the dative of wer — “to whom”; the case alone carries what English marks with a preposition.

sentences.t: Da sprach der dritte „Vater, laßt mich auch einmal gewähren,“
sentences.l: Then spoke the third “father, let me too have my way for once,”
sentences.i: Then the third said: “Father, let me have my turn too,”
sentences.n: “laßt” is the plural imperative: the son addresses his father as “ihr,” the older respectful form used to a parent. “einen gewähren lassen” is to let someone do as he will.

sentences.t: und weil es anfieng zu regnen, zog er seinen Degen und schwenkte ihn in Kreuzhieben über seinen Kopf, daß kein Tropfen auf ihn fiel:
sentences.l: and because it began to rain, he drew his rapier and swung it in cross-strokes over his head, so that not a drop fell on him:
sentences.i: and since it had begun to rain, he drew his rapier and swept it in cross-strokes above his head, so that not a drop fell on him:
sentences.n: “anfieng” is the 1857 spelling of anfing (anfangen, to begin) — the ie for i runs all through this edition (gieng, fieng, hieng). “daß” after a main clause commonly marks the result: so that.

sentences.t: und als der Regen stärker ward, und endlich so stark, als ob man mit Mulden vom Himmel göße, schwang er den Degen immer schneller und blieb so trocken, als säß er unter Dach und Fach.
sentences.l: and as the rain grew stronger, and at last so strong as if one poured from heaven with troughs, he swung the rapier ever faster and stayed as dry as if he sat under roof and rafter.
sentences.i: and as the rain grew heavier, and at last so heavy that it seemed to be emptied from heaven by the tubful, he swung the rapier faster and faster and stayed as dry as though he were sitting indoors.
sentences.n: “ward” is the old past of werden (modern wurde). A Mulde is a wooden trough; the picture is of rain tipped out by the troughful. “als ob man … göße” and “als säß er” are subjunctives of comparison — as if one were pouring, as if he were sitting. “Dach und Fach” is a set phrase for a house’s roof and framing: safe under cover.

sentences.t: Wie der Vater das sah, erstaunte er und sprach „du hast das beste Meisterstück gemacht, das Haus ist dein.“
sentences.l: When the father saw that, he was astonished and spoke “you have made the best masterpiece, the house is yours.”
sentences.i: When the father saw that, he was amazed, and said: “You have made the best masterpiece; the house is yours.”
sentences.n: “wie” at the head of a clause means “when,” as often in these tales.

sentences.t: Die beiden andern Brüder waren damit zufrieden, wie sie vorher gelobt hatten, und weil sie sich einander so lieb hatten, blieben sie alle drei zusammen im Haus und trieben ihr Handwerk;
sentences.l: The two other brothers were content with that, as they had promised beforehand, and because they had one another so dear, all three stayed together in the house and plied their trade;
sentences.i: The other two brothers were content with that, as they had promised beforehand, and because they loved one another so well, all three stayed together in the house and plied their trades;
sentences.n: “geloben” is to vow or pledge — a shade more solemn than versprechen, and not loben, to praise. “sich lieb haben” — to hold one another dear; German says it with haben where English uses a verb of loving. “ein Handwerk treiben” is to carry on a trade.

sentences.t: und da sie so gut ausgelernt hatten und so geschickt waren, verdienten sie viel Geld.
sentences.l: and since they had learned out so well and were so skilled, they earned much money.
sentences.i: and since they had served out their training so well and were so skilful, they earned a great deal of money.
sentences.n: “auslernen” is to finish one’s apprenticeship — the point at which an apprentice becomes a journeyman; the particle aus carries “to the end.”

sentences.t: So lebten sie vergnügt bis in ihr Alter zusammen, und als der eine krank ward und starb, grämten sich die zwei andern so sehr darüber, daß sie auch krank wurden und bald starben.
sentences.l: So they lived contentedly together into their old age, and when the one grew sick and died, the two others grieved themselves so much over it that they too grew sick and soon died.
sentences.i: So they lived contentedly together into their old age; and when one of them fell sick and died, the other two grieved so bitterly over it that they too fell sick and soon died.
sentences.n: “sich grämen” is reflexive — one grieves oneself; “darüber” gathers up the thing grieved over. “ward” again for wurde.

sentences.t: Da wurden sie, weil sie so geschickt gewesen waren und sich so lieb gehabt hatten, alle drei zusammen in ein Grab gelegt.
sentences.l: Then they were, because they had been so skilled and had held one another so dear, all three laid together in one grave.
sentences.i: And so, because they had been so skilful and had loved one another so well, all three were laid together in one grave.
sentences.n: A passive built with werden — “wurden … gelegt,” were laid — with the whole reason-clause packed in between the auxiliary and the participle, which is where German likes to put it.

glossary.alter: das Alter — old age (“bis in ihr Alter” = into their old age); also alter — old (adj., masc. infl.)
glossary.beschlagen: beschlagen — to shoe (a horse) (infinitive); also the past participle, shod, studded
glossary.es: es — it (here the impersonal es: ‘es war ein Mann’, ‘es traf sich’, ‘es währte nicht lang’)
glossary.euch: euch — you (acc./dat. pl.; here a father to his three sons)
glossary.gelobt: geloben — promised, vowed (past participle; not loben, to praise)
glossary.hieb: der Hieb — blow, stroke, cut (masc.; also hieb = hauen, hewed, past sg.)
glossary.jagen: das Jagen — the racing, galloping (infinitive used as a noun; “in vollem Jagen” = at full gallop); as a verb jagen — to chase, race
glossary.jagte: jagen — raced, galloped on (3rd sg. past; here intransitive, of a horse at full gallop)
glossary.laufe: der Lauf — run, running (dat. sg.; “in vollem Laufe” = at full run)
glossary.pferde: das Pferd — horses (acc. pl.; ‘des Königs Pferde’); also dat. sg., dem Pferde
glossary.regen: der Regen — rain (masc.); also regen — to stir, move
glossary.sollt: sollen — shall, are to (2nd pl.; ‘nun sollt ihr sehen’ = now you shall see)
glossary.trieben: treiben — plied, carried on (3rd pl. past; “ein Handwerk treiben” = to ply a trade)
glossary.versucht: versuchen — try yourselves, see what you can do (imperative pl.); also versucht — tried (past part.)
glossary.weiß: wissen — (I) know (1st sg. pres.; ‘ich weiß nicht’); also weiß — white (adj.)
glossary.wo: wo — when, of a point in time (‘die Zeit, wo …’ = the time when); also wo — where
glossary.zog: ziehen — drew (3rd sg. past; ‘zog seinen Degen’ = drew his rapier)
glossary.zogen: ziehen — set off, travelled away (3rd pl. past; “zogen fort” = fortziehen)
